newsitem.title: USA: Mexico needs momentum to keep up recovery - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico needs momentum to keep up recovery - analysts.

text.p: Mexico needs fresh momentum to keep the economic recovery on track during the political process leading up to its mid-year congressional and local elections, a group of experts said in a panel discussion.

Walter Molano, director of economic and financial research as SBC Warburg Inc, said he doubted the export-led growth in 1996 could be sustained because maquiladoras -- duty free assembly plants -- are operating close to full capacity, and the new momentum would have to come from the consumer sector, where wages remain depressed. "Mexico is at an important juncture to move ahead or to slow down," he said.

The government's 1997 projection of 4.5 percent growth, 15 percent inflation and an average peso value of 8.5 per U.S. dollar, is not totally convincing, said Roberto Salinas Leon, executive director of the Mexico-City based Centro de Investigaciones Sobre la Libre Empresa.

To maintain the projected growth rate and currency value, inflation would have to exceed the target, while low inflation and parity would choke off growth, he said during the panel discussion, which was sponsored by the Americas Society.

Juan Enriquez Cabot, a visiting fellow at Harvard University's Center for International Affairs, warned that many Mexican voters are seething with anger and frustration as a result of the painful 1995 recession and recovery.
"It is important to channel the discontent through the political process," he said.

Molano predicted that the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) would retain its majority in Congress in the coming election, but said the PRI needs 43 percent of support and the latest polls showed it has only 38 percent.
Given the party's large war chest, acquiring another five percent of the vote is not a serious challenge, he said.

Salinas said even if the PRI loses the absolute majority and ends up sharing the legislative power with the right-of-the center National Action Party (PAN) in Congress, the free-market reform would continue.
The real test will come in the presidential elections in 2000, he said.
